engXQtTh: "I told the truth even though it cost me my place on the team." Which theme best matches the quotation?
Choosing truth despite a personal cost shows the theme of honesty.
"She shared her last sandwich with the new kid who had forgotten his lunch." Which theme best matches the quotation?
Giving up something to help another person shows kindness.
"He promised to keep my secret, then told the whole class by lunch." Which theme best matches the quotation?
Breaking a promise of trust is betrayal.
"No matter what happened, I knew my best friend would stand beside me." Which theme best matches the quotation?
Always standing by someone shows loyalty.
"I was angry for a long time, but finally I decided to let it go and shake his hand." Which theme best matches the quotation?
Letting go of anger toward someone who hurt you is forgiveness.
"He had more gold than he could ever spend, yet he still wanted more." Which theme best matches the quotation?
Always wanting more wealth than you need shows greed.
"Every time she won an award, I felt a sour twist in my stomach." Which theme best matches the quotation?
Feeling bitter about someone else's success is jealousy.
"Even after the fire took our home, Mom said we would plant a new garden in spring." Which theme best matches the quotation?
Looking forward to a better future after loss shows hope.
"I moved to a new city where no one knew my name, and the hallways felt endless." Which theme best matches the quotation?
Feeling unknown and isolated in a new place shows loneliness.
"I fell off the bike twenty times, but on the twenty-first try I rode to the end of the street." Which theme best matches the quotation?
Continuing to try after many failures is perseverance.
"Grandpa's old stories taught me where our family came from and who I am." Which theme best matches the quotation?
Learning about family roots and who you are reflects identity and heritage.
"I thought I was too important to ask for help — until I failed the test." Which theme best matches the quotation?
Being too proud and then failing shows that pride comes before a fall.
"The townspeople built a fence to keep out the strangers, but the strangers only wanted to trade." Which theme best matches the quotation?
Judging and excluding strangers without knowing them shows prejudice.
"By the end of the summer, I was no longer the shy kid who hid behind Mom." Which theme best matches the quotation?
Changing from a shy child into someone more confident reflects growing up.
"He swore he would make them pay for what they had done to his brother." Which theme best matches the quotation?
Wanting to make someone pay for a wrong is revenge.
"Alone, none of us could lift the canoe; together, we carried it to the lake." Which theme best matches the quotation?
Accomplishing something only by working together shows teamwork.
"The forest gave us food and shelter, so we promised to take only what we needed." Which theme best matches the quotation?
Taking only what is needed from the forest shows respect for nature.
"My hands shook as I stepped onto the stage, but I sang the first note anyway." Which theme best matches the quotation?
"I gave away my winter coat because the man on the corner had none." Which theme best matches the quotation?
Freely giving something valuable to someone in need shows generosity.
"We argued about everything, but when she moved away, I missed her every day." Which theme best matches the quotation?
Missing someone deeply despite disagreements shows the value of friendship.
"I wanted to be the first in my family to graduate from university, and nothing would stop me." Which theme best matches the quotation?
A strong drive to achieve a big goal is ambition.
"The king had every treasure, yet he sat alone in his castle, wishing for a single friend." Which theme best matches the quotation?
A rich but lonely king shows that wealth cannot buy happiness.
engTnCp: Which word best describes the tone? The old house stood empty now, its windows dark, its garden overgrown with the weeds of forgotten summers.
Words like empty, dark and forgotten create a sad, serious tone.
Which word best describes the tone? I still remember the smell of Grandma's kitchen on Sunday mornings, when the whole family crowded around her table.
Fondly remembering the past creates a nostalgic tone.
Which word best describes the tone? My dog believes he is a lion. He roars at squirrels, then hides behind the couch when the vacuum turns on.
The funny contrast between a 'lion' and a scared dog creates a humorous tone.
Which word best describes the tone? Oh, wonderful — my phone died right before the bus driver asked for my e-ticket. What perfect timing.
Saying 'wonderful' and 'perfect' about a bad situation is sarcasm.
Which word best describes the tone? This is unacceptable. The city promised to fix the bridge two years ago, and still nothing has been done!
Words like unacceptable and the exclamation show anger.
Which word best describes the tone? The lake was still. A loon called once across the water, and the mist drifted slowly over the pines.
Quiet images like a still lake and drifting mist create a peaceful tone.
Which word best describes the tone? Every creak of the floorboards made my heart race. Was someone else in the house?
The creaks, racing heart and question build suspense.
Which word best describes the tone? We did it! After months of fundraising, the new playground is finally open for every child in town!
The exclamations and good news create a joyful tone.
Which word best describes the tone? Of course they gave the award to the coach's son. Hard work clearly means nothing around here.
The resentful complaint about unfairness creates a bitter tone.
Which word best describes the tone? Researchers measured the ice thickness at twelve sites between January and March.
The sentence reports facts without emotion, so the tone is objective.
Which word best describes the tone? What if I forget my lines? What if everyone laughs? The curtain rises in five minutes.
The worried questions and countdown create an anxious tone.
Which word best describes the tone? Each of you has the power to change this community. Stand up, speak out, and make your voice heard!
Encouraging commands that urge action create an inspiring tone.
Which word best describes the tone? The soldiers who never came home deserve our silence and our gratitude each November.
Honouring fallen soldiers with silence and gratitude creates a deeply respectful, reverent tone.
Which word best describes the tone? Congratulations to the team that managed to lose the game in the final three seconds. Truly impressive work.
Praising a loss as 'impressive' is sarcasm.
Which word best describes the tone? The snow has been falling for days, and the town has gone quiet; no cars, no voices, only the wind.
The empty, silent town creates a lonely, desolate tone.
Which word best describes the tone? Look out, world! I just learned to tie my own shoes, and next I'm going to learn to fly a rocket!
The silly, exaggerated boast gives a lighthearted, playful tone.
Which word best describes the tone? Despite the setbacks, our scientists believe a cure is within reach, and every test brings us closer.
Belief that a cure is near creates a hopeful tone.
Which word best describes the tone? You will clean your room tonight. No excuses, no arguments, and no video games until it is done.
Firm commands with no room for argument create a stern tone.
Which word best describes the tone? Back then, we rode our bikes until the streetlights came on, and summer seemed to last forever.
Longing memories of childhood summers create a nostalgic tone.
Which word best describes the tone? I can't believe it — a real letter from the astronaut, signed and addressed to me!
The exclamation and amazement show an excited tone.
Which word best describes the tone? The funeral was small. A few friends stood in the rain and spoke softly of the man they had loved.
The funeral, rain and soft voices create a sad, serious tone.
Which word best describes the tone? The new policy is reasonable in some ways, but it raises questions that the council has not yet answered.
Balancing approval with doubts creates a careful, cautious tone.
engXAuPv: Homework every night leaves students with no time to rest, play or spend with family. Schools should cut it back. What is the author's point of view about homework?
There is too much and it should be reduced
Students need more homework
Homework has no effect
Homework should be done on weekends only
The author says homework takes away free time and should be cut back.
Uniforms save families money and stop students from judging each other by their clothes. What is the author's point of view about school uniforms?
Uniforms are a good idea
Uniforms are too expensive
Uniforms make students judge each other
Uniforms should be banned
The author lists only benefits of uniforms.
A tablet can never replace the feel of a real book in your hands, the smell of the pages, and the joy of turning them. How does the author view printed books?
Printed books offer something tablets cannot
Tablets are better than books
Books are outdated
Books and tablets are exactly the same
The author praises the special experience of real books.
Our town's new skatepark gives teens a safe place to gather, and police report fewer complaints since it opened. What is the author's point of view about the skatepark?
It has been good for the town
It has caused more problems
It is unsafe for teens
It should be closed
The author points to safety and fewer complaints as benefits.
I know many people love fireworks, but they terrify pets and wildlife. A quiet laser show would be kinder. What is the author's point of view about fireworks?
They should be replaced with something quieter
They are harmless to animals
There should be more fireworks
Laser shows are frightening
The author argues fireworks harm animals and suggests a quieter option.
Some say cellphones distract students, but used wisely, they let students look up facts and contact family in emergencies. How does the author view cellphones at school?
They can be useful if used wisely
They should be banned completely
They are only distracting
They are useful only for games
The author admits a concern but focuses on wise, helpful uses.
Every piece of litter on our beaches ends up hurting fish and birds. We all must pick up after ourselves. What is the author's point of view about litter?
People must take responsibility for it
Litter is not a real problem
Only cities should clean beaches
Fish are not affected by litter
The author says everyone must pick up litter because it harms wildlife.
Learning a second language opens doors to new friends, new jobs and new ways of seeing the world. What is the author's point of view about learning a second language?
It brings many benefits
It is a waste of time
It is too difficult for most people
It only helps with travel
The author lists many benefits of a second language.
Camping in the rain is my idea of a nightmare: soggy socks, a leaky tent and cold canned beans. How does the author feel about camping in the rain?
The author strongly dislikes it
The author loves it
The author has never tried it
The author thinks it is relaxing
Calling it a nightmare and listing complaints shows dislike.
Fast food may be quick, but its salt and fat add up. A home-cooked meal is worth the extra time. What is the author's point of view about fast food?
Home-cooked meals are a better choice
Fast food is the healthiest option
Cooking takes too long to be worth it
Salt and fat are good for you
The author argues home cooking is worth the time compared with fast food.
Our library's new sci-fi section is small but growing, and I can't wait to see what they add next month. How does the author view the new sci-fi section?
The author is excited about it
The author thinks it is useless
The author wants it removed
The author is bored by it
Saying 'I can't wait' shows excitement.
Year-round school would end the 'summer slide,' when students forget much of what they learned. What is the author's point of view about year-round school?
It would help students keep their learning
It would make students forget more
Summer holidays should be longer
It would have no effect
The author says year-round school would stop forgetting over summer.
Zoos claim to protect animals, but no enclosure can match the freedom of the open savanna. What is the author's point of view about zoos?
Zoos cannot give animals true freedom
Zoos are better than the wild
Zoos always protect animals perfectly
The savanna is dangerous for animals
The author doubts zoos and says enclosures cannot match the wild.
Social media lets me keep in touch with cousins overseas, though I try to limit my scrolling to an hour a day. How does the author view social media?
It is useful when used in moderation
It should be avoided completely
More scrolling is always better
It is only for strangers
The author values it for family contact but limits its use.
Recess should never be taken away as punishment; children need movement to learn well. What is the author's point of view about recess?
Recess is necessary and should not be removed
Recess wastes learning time
Recess is a fair punishment
Children learn better sitting still
The author says children need recess to learn.
The new mall has stores, sure, but it paved over the only forest in our neighbourhood. How does the author view the new mall?
The author regrets the loss of the forest
The author is thrilled about the stores
The author wants more malls
The author did not notice any change
The author focuses on the forest that was lost.
Volunteering at the food bank taught me more about my community than any textbook ever could. What is the author's point of view about volunteering?
It is a valuable learning experience
It is boring and pointless
Textbooks teach more
Food banks do not need help
The author says volunteering taught more than textbooks.
Hockey may be Canada's game, but soccer is cheaper to play and needs only a ball and some open space. What is the author's point of view about soccer?
Soccer is more accessible than hockey
Hockey is cheaper than soccer
Soccer needs special equipment
Soccer is not played in Canada
The author points out soccer is cheaper and needs little equipment.
Electric buses are quieter and cleaner. Our city should replace its diesel fleet as soon as possible. What is the author's point of view about electric buses?
The city should switch to them soon
Diesel buses are better
Electric buses are too loud
Buses should be removed entirely
The author calls for replacing diesel buses quickly.
I used to think poetry was boring, but after reading a few modern poems, I've changed my mind. How does the author now feel about poetry?
The author has come to appreciate it
The author still finds it boring
The author has never read poetry
The author only likes old poems
The author says they changed their mind after reading modern poems.
Daylight saving time throws off our sleep twice a year for very little benefit. It is time to end it. What is the author's point of view about daylight saving time?
It should be ended
It should happen more often
It helps people sleep better
It has huge benefits
The author says it disrupts sleep for little benefit and should end.
Online classes gave me flexibility, but I missed laughing with friends in the hallway. How does the author view online classes?
They had both advantages and drawbacks
They were perfect in every way
They were completely terrible
They were exactly like in-person school
The author mentions flexibility as a plus and missing friends as a minus.
engXFgCl: Which figure of speech is used? The classroom was a zoo after the fire drill.
It says the classroom was a zoo without using like or as, so it is a metaphor.
Which figure of speech is used? The thunder grumbled angrily in the distance.
Thunder cannot grumble angrily; giving it human feelings is personification.
Which figure of speech is used? Seven silly snakes slithered south.
Repeating the s sound at the start of words is alliteration.
Which figure of speech is used? The bacon sizzled in the pan.
Sizzled imitates the sound it names, so it is onomatopoeia.
Which figure of speech is used? My backpack weighs a tonne!
A backpack does not weigh a tonne; the exaggeration is hyperbole.
Which figure of speech is used? His smile was as bright as the morning sun.
It compares using as, so it is a simile.
Which figure of speech is used? The leaves danced in the autumn wind.
Leaves cannot dance; giving them a human action is personification.
Which figure of speech is used? Time is a thief that steals our youth.
Time is called a thief directly, without like or as, which is a metaphor.
Which figure of speech is used? I've told you a million times to close the door!
No one says something a million times; this exaggeration is hyperbole.
Which figure of speech is used? The snow fell like soft feathers.
It compares snow to feathers using like, so it is a simile.
Which figure of speech is used? Crack! The branch broke under the weight of the ice.
Crack imitates the sound of breaking, so it is onomatopoeia.
Which figure of speech is used? Big brown bears bounced on blue balloons.
The repeated b sound at the start of words is alliteration.
Which figure of speech is used? The old door complained loudly when we pushed it open.
Doors cannot complain; giving one a human action is personification.
Which figure of speech is used? Her voice was music to his ears.
Her voice is called music directly, which is a metaphor.
Which figure of speech is used? The baby was as quiet as a mouse.
It compares using as, so it is a simile.
Which figure of speech is used? This line is so long it stretches to the moon.
A line cannot reach the moon; the exaggeration is hyperbole.
Which figure of speech is used? The bees went buzz around the flowers.
Buzz imitates the bees' sound, so it is onomatopoeia.
Which figure of speech is used? Peter's pet parrot prefers peanuts.
The repeated p sound at the start of words is alliteration.
Which figure of speech is used? The stars winked at us from the night sky.
Stars cannot wink; that human action makes it personification.
Which figure of speech is used? He ran like the wind to catch the bus.
It compares his running to the wind using like, so it is a simile.
Which figure of speech is used? My brother is a couch potato on weekends.
Calling him a couch potato without like or as is a metaphor.
Which figure of speech is used? I'm so tired I could sleep for a year.
No one sleeps for a year; the exaggeration is hyperbole.
engArgT: In an argument about school uniforms, what role does this sentence play? Our school should require students to wear uniforms.
This is the main position the writer wants readers to accept.
In an argument about school uniforms, what role does this sentence play? Uniforms reduce peer pressure about clothing brands.
It explains why the writer supports uniforms.
In an argument about school uniforms, what role does this sentence play? A survey of 500 schools found that bullying about clothing dropped by 30% after uniforms were introduced.
A survey result is factual support for the reason.
In an argument about school uniforms, what role does this sentence play? Some argue that uniforms limit students' self-expression.
It presents the opposing side's view.
In an argument about banning plastic bags, what role does this sentence play? Our city should ban single-use plastic bags.
This is the writer's main position.
In an argument about banning plastic bags, what role does this sentence play? Plastic bags harm wildlife in lakes and oceans.
It gives a general reason for the ban.
In an argument about banning plastic bags, what role does this sentence play? The Government of Canada estimates that Canadians use up to 15 billion plastic bags each year.
A statistic from a source supports the reason.
In an argument about banning plastic bags, what role does this sentence play? Opponents say paper bags use more energy to produce.
It presents an objection from the other side.
In an argument about a four-day school week, what role does this sentence play? Schools should switch to a four-day week.
This is the main position being argued.
In an argument about a four-day school week, what role does this sentence play? A shorter week would give students more time to rest and recharge.
It explains why the writer supports the change.
In an argument about a four-day school week, what role does this sentence play? In one Colorado district, attendance rose by 5% after the four-day week began.
A specific measured result is evidence.
In an argument about a four-day school week, what role does this sentence play? Critics point out that working parents would need extra child care on the fifth day.
It gives the opposing side's concern.
In an argument about video games in class, what role does this sentence play? Teachers should use educational video games in class.
This is the writer's central position.
In an argument about video games in class, what role does this sentence play? Games keep students engaged and motivated to learn.
It explains why games should be used.
In an argument about video games in class, what role does this sentence play? A university study found students using math games scored 12% higher on tests.
A study result is factual support.
In an argument about video games in class, what role does this sentence play? Some parents worry that games add to screen time.
In an argument about lowering the voting age, what role does this sentence play? The voting age in Canada should be lowered to 16.
This is the main position of the argument.
In an argument about lowering the voting age, what role does this sentence play? Sixteen-year-olds pay taxes on their part-time jobs and should have a say in government.
It explains why the voting age should change.
In an argument about lowering the voting age, what role does this sentence play? In Austria, where 16-year-olds can vote, turnout among first-time voters has been comparable to older age groups.
A factual observation from a real example supports the reason.
In an argument about lowering the voting age, what role does this sentence play? Opponents argue that most 16-year-olds are not yet informed about politics.
It presents the other side's objection.
In an argument about community gardens, what role does this sentence play? Every neighbourhood should have a community garden.
In an argument about community gardens, what role does this sentence play? Some residents fear the gardens will attract pests.
It raises an objection from those who disagree.
engXCmpG: Poem: "The beaver builds with patient paws, / a lodge of sticks by nature's laws." Encyclopedia entry: "Beavers build lodges from branches and mud, with underwater entrances for safety." How do the texts treat beavers differently?
The poem uses rhythm and rhyme; the entry gives facts
Both give facts in plain sentences
The entry rhymes; the poem does not
Neither mentions lodges
The poem has rhyme and rhythm, while the encyclopedia states facts plainly.

Diary entry: "June 3 — I finally saw the northern lights tonight! I cried, it was so beautiful." News report: "Strong solar activity produced northern lights visible across the Prairies on Monday." What is a key difference?
The diary shares personal feelings; the report states facts
Both share personal feelings
The report uses the first person
The diary explains solar activity
A diary is personal and emotional, while a news report is factual and impersonal.
Fable: "The tortoise beat the hare because slow and steady wins the race." Biology article: "Tortoises can live for over 100 years and move at about 0.3 km/h." What does each text mainly offer?
The fable teaches a lesson; the article gives information
Both teach a moral lesson
The article tells a story about a race
The fable gives speed measurements
Fables teach morals, while articles inform with facts.

Letter: "Dear Aunt Rosa, the trip to Banff was amazing — you have to see Lake Louise!" Travel brochure: "Visit Lake Louise, open year-round, with canoe rentals from May to October." How do the purposes differ?
The letter shares an experience with one person; the brochure persuades and informs many readers
Both are written to one family member
The brochure describes a personal trip
The letter lists rental dates
A personal letter shares experiences with one person, while a brochure targets the public.

Poem: "The city never sleeps; / its lights blink like a thousand eyes." Textbook: "Cities use large amounts of electricity at night for street lighting and buildings." How does each text describe city lights?
The poem uses figurative language; the textbook uses literal facts
Both use figurative language
The textbook uses a simile
The poem gives electricity statistics
The poem compares lights to eyes, while the textbook states facts literally.

Biography: "Terry Fox was born in Winnipeg in 1958 and began his Marathon of Hope in 1980." Song lyric: "He ran with one leg and a heart full of hope, / across the land that he loved." How do the texts differ?
The biography gives dates and facts; the song expresses emotion
Both list exact dates
The song gives his birthplace
The biography uses rhyme
Biographies give factual details, while songs use emotional, poetic language.

Comic strip: a cat thinks in a bubble, "Monday again? Wake me on Friday." Editorial: "The four-day work week could improve worker happiness and productivity." How do the genres share ideas differently?
The comic uses humour and pictures; the editorial uses reasoned argument
Both use thought bubbles
The editorial uses a cartoon cat
The comic presents statistics
Comics use humour and images, while editorials argue with reasons.

Legend: "Long ago, the Great Spirit placed the Thousand Islands like scattered flowers in the river." Geography text: "The Thousand Islands were shaped by glaciers that scraped and exposed ancient rock." How do the texts explain the islands?
The legend gives a traditional explanation; the text gives a scientific one
Both describe glaciers
The geography text tells about the Great Spirit
Both are scientific reports
Legends explain through traditional stories, while geography texts use science.
Recipe: "Whisk two eggs, add milk, and pour onto a hot pan." Story: "Dad whisked the eggs, humming his favourite song, as the smell of pancakes filled the house." What is a key difference?
The recipe gives steps; the story creates a scene
Both give numbered steps
The recipe describes Dad humming
The story lists exact amounts
Recipes instruct, while stories describe characters and settings.

Interview: "Q: Why did you become a firefighter? A: I wanted to help people on their worst days." Short story: "Jamal pulled on his helmet, remembering the fire that had once saved his family's lives." How do the texts present a firefighter?
The interview uses a real person's answers; the story invents a character
Both use questions and answers
The story is a real interview
The interview invents a fictional hero
Interviews record real answers, while short stories create fictional characters.
Haiku: "Spring rain on the roof / tapping softly through the night / seeds wake in the dark." Weather report: "Expect 15 mm of rain overnight, clearing by morning." How do the texts treat rain?
The haiku creates a mood; the report gives a forecast
Both measure rainfall
The report counts syllables
The haiku predicts tomorrow's weather
The haiku uses imagery to create mood, while the report gives measurable predictions.
Advertisement: "Zoom Sneakers — run faster than ever!" Consumer review: "The sneakers were comfortable, but the soles wore out after three months." How do the texts differ in purpose?
The ad tries to sell; the review evaluates honestly
Both try to sell the shoes
The review exaggerates the shoes' speed
The ad points out problems
Ads aim to persuade buyers, while reviews judge the product's strengths and weaknesses.
Play script: "NARRATOR: The storm grew louder. (Thunder sound effect.)" Novel: "The storm grew louder, and thunder shook the windows of the old farmhouse." How do the genres show the storm?
The script uses stage directions; the novel describes it in narration
Both use sound-effect cues
The novel has a narrator label
Neither mentions thunder
Scripts rely on cues for performance, while novels describe events in prose.

Speech: "Friends, we must protect our rivers — for our children and theirs!" Science report: "Tests showed nitrate levels in the river were twice the safe limit." How do the texts address river pollution?
The speech appeals to emotion; the report presents data
Both present test results
The report speaks to friends
The speech lists nitrate levels
Speeches often use emotional appeals, while reports present data.
Graphic novel panel: a girl stares at a huge wave, with the caption "Now or never." Poem: "The wave rose high, a wall of grey, / and still she would not turn away." How do the texts show her courage?
The graphic novel uses an image and caption; the poem uses rhyming lines
Both are only pictures
The poem uses speech bubbles
The graphic novel uses rhyme
Graphic novels combine images and short text, while poems use language patterns like rhyme.
Myth: "Thor's hammer strikes the clouds, and thunder rolls across the sky." Science text: "Thunder is the sound of air expanding rapidly when heated by lightning." How do the texts explain thunder?
The myth uses gods; the science text uses physical causes
Both describe air expanding
The science text mentions Thor
Both are traditional stories
Myths explain nature through gods, while science explains physical causes.

Personal essay: "I was nervous on my first day at a new school, but a girl named Priya waved me over." Guidebook: "New students should report to the main office and pick up a timetable." How do the texts differ?
The essay tells a personal experience; the guidebook gives instructions
Both give instructions
The guidebook describes Priya
The essay lists office hours
Personal essays share experiences, while guidebooks tell readers what to do.

Tall tale: "Paul Bunyan dug the Great Lakes so his blue ox, Babe, would have water to drink." Geography text: "The Great Lakes formed as glaciers melted at the end of the last ice age." How do the texts differ?
The tall tale uses exaggeration; the text gives a scientific explanation
Both describe melting glaciers
The text mentions Babe the ox
The tall tale gives exact dates
Tall tales exaggerate for entertainment, while geography texts explain with science.
Poem: "My grandmother's hands, / wrinkled maps of every road she travelled." Obituary: "Rosa Lee, 92, worked as a nurse for 40 years and raised five children." How do the texts present a grandmother?
The poem uses metaphor; the obituary gives life facts
Both use metaphor
The obituary compares hands to maps
The poem lists her age and job
The poem calls her hands maps, while the obituary lists facts about her life.
Instruction manual: "Step 3: Attach the wheels using the four bolts." Adventure story: "With the last bolt tightened, Eli's homemade go-kart was ready for the big hill." How do the texts differ?
The manual tells how to do a task; the story tells what a character experiences
Both are numbered steps
The manual describes Eli's feelings
The story lists the parts needed
Manuals give procedures, while stories focus on characters and events.

Blog post: "Honestly, the new library is the best thing to happen to our town in years!" Council report: "The library opened on March 1 and recorded 4,200 visits in its first month." How do the texts differ in style?
The blog is informal and opinionated; the report is formal and factual
Both are formal and factual
The report gives the writer's opinion
The blog only lists visit numbers
Blogs are often casual and personal, while official reports are formal and factual.
Lullaby: "Hush now, little one, the moon is watching you." Astronomy article: "The Moon is about 384,400 km from Earth and reflects light from the Sun." How do the texts treat the Moon?
The lullaby uses personification to comfort; the article gives scientific facts
Both give the Moon's distance
The article personifies the Moon
The lullaby explains reflected light
The lullaby gives the Moon human qualities, while the article provides measurable facts.
engXLhIl: One illustration of the Last Spike in 1885 shows a crowd of officials in top hats cheering. Another shows exhausted Chinese railway workers resting beside the tracks. What does the second illustration emphasize?
The workers whose labour built the railway
The officials' celebration
The fancy clothing of the crowd
How easy the work was
Showing tired workers draws attention to the people who did the hard labour.
Two illustrations of Little Red Riding Hood show the wolf. In one, he is a cartoon with a goofy grin; in the other, he looms in dark shadows with glowing eyes. How do the two versions differ in mood?
One is playful; the other is frightening
Both are frightening
Both are playful
Neither shows the wolf
A goofy cartoon feels playful, while shadows and glowing eyes create fear.

A painting shows Jacques Cartier proudly planting a cross at Gaspé in 1534, with Iroquoian people in the background. A modern illustration shows the same scene from the viewpoint of Chief Donnacona, looking worried. What does the modern illustration add?
The Indigenous perspective on the event
A celebration of Cartier's ship
A map of France
The weather that day
Showing the scene through Donnacona's eyes adds the Indigenous viewpoint left out of the older painting.
In one illustration of Robin Hood, he is shown laughing with his merry men around a feast. In another, he aims an arrow from a tree with a serious face. What does each illustration focus on?
One shows his friendships; the other his skill and danger
Both show him eating
Both show him in a tree
Neither shows Robin Hood
The feast highlights friendship, while the aimed arrow highlights skill and danger.
One illustration of the Titanic shows the grand ship sailing proudly in sunshine. Another shows lifeboats in dark, icy water. What does the second illustration emphasize?
The tragedy of the sinking
The ship's luxury
A calm summer voyage
